clinicalPearls: The eyelid margin turns outward away from the globe, most often affecting the lower lid, leading to tearing, irritation, and a red, exposed conjunctiva
Involutional ectropion from age-related horizontal lid laxity is the commonest form
Paralytic ectropion follows facial nerve palsy with loss of orbicularis tone and is often accompanied by lagophthalmos
Cicatricial ectropion results from vertical shortening of the anterior lamella due to skin scarring, burns, or actinic damage
Chronic exposure causes conjunctival keratinisation, punctal eversion with epiphora, and risk of exposure keratopathy
Interim management centres on lubrication and protecting the ocular surface, with taping or moisture chambers for exposure
Definitive treatment is surgical and directed at the specific cause, such as lid-tightening for involutional disease or skin grafting for cicatricial cases
reference.pathophysiology: Ectropion is outward rotation of the eyelid margin. Involutional ectropion stems from horizontal lid laxity and weakening of the canthal tendons and retractors with age. Paralytic ectropion follows loss of orbicularis oculi function in facial nerve palsy, so the lid sags and everts. Cicatricial ectropion arises when scarring and contracture of the eyelid skin (anterior lamella) mechanically pull the margin away from the eye. Mechanical ectropion is caused by a mass or oedema everting the lid. Eversion disrupts the normal tear drainage and exposes the cornea and conjunctiva to drying and keratinisation.
additionalDifferentials: Involutional versus cicatricial versus paralytic subtypes
Mechanical eversion from an eyelid or orbital mass
Punctal stenosis as an alternative cause of epiphora
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination to assess corneal exposure and conjunctival keratinisation
Fluorescein staining to detect exposure keratopathy
Assessment of lid laxity and canthal tendon integrity
Evaluation of facial nerve function in suspected paralytic ectropion
Examination of eyelid skin for scarring or actinic change in cicatricial cases
redFlags: Exposure keratopathy with corneal breakdown threatening vision, particularly with associated lagophthalmos
New facial nerve palsy requiring evaluation of its cause
A causative eyelid mass needing exclusion of malignancy
Progressive cicatricial change from an underlying dermatological or systemic disorder
reference.prognosis: Surgical correction usually restores lid position and relieves symptoms with good outcomes; untreated ectropion can lead to persistent epiphora, chronic conjunctival changes, and exposure-related corneal damage.
pitfalls: Managing epiphora without recognising the underlying lid malposition
Overlooking corneal exposure in paralytic ectropion until keratopathy develops
Failing to address anterior lamella shortening in cicatricial cases, leading to recurrence
Missing an eyelid tumour causing mechanical eversion
management: Definitive treatment is surgical correction tailored to cause, using horizontal lid tightening such as a lateral tarsal strip for involutional disease and skin grafting or flaps to release cicatricial ectropion
Protect the ocular surface with lubricating drops and ointment, moisture chambers and lid taping as interim and adjunctive care
For paralytic ectropion, treat the underlying facial nerve palsy and guard against lagophthalmos-related exposure with taping and, where needed, canthoplasty
Relieve mechanical ectropion by removing or treating the causative mass or oedema
Actively treat exposure keratopathy and monitor with slit-lamp examination and fluorescein staining to prevent corneal damage
Refer to ophthalmology or oculoplastic surgery for assessment and surgical planning
